props.title: Frozen
props.initialSlug: Three friends trapped on a ski lift face deadly cold

sections.content: Let's be clear - Frozen (2010) is not Disney's beloved musical, but a brutally tense survival horror film that turns a simple ski lift scenario into 90 minutes of escalating dread. Director Adam Green crafts a minimalist nightmare that shares DNA with other single-location thrillers like Open Water (2003) and 127 Hours (2010). The film's premise is deceptively simple - three skiers stranded on a chairlift - but Green maximizes the psychological terror and physical threats, from frostbite to circling wolves.

sections.content: The film exemplifies the "elevated survival horror" trend that gained momentum in the 2010s. Like The Shallows (2016) and Crawl (2019), it takes a primal fear - in this case, being trapped at heights in freezing conditions - and explores how ordinary people react under extreme duress. The practical effects and real location shooting at Utah's Snowbasin Resort add crushing authenticity to every frozen breath and frostbitten limb.

Green's direction keeps the tension mounting through clever use of limited space. Similar to Buried (2010) and Phone Booth (2002), the restricted setting becomes a pressure cooker for character development. The film's sound design deserves special mention - the creaking metal, howling wind, and distant wolf calls create a sonic landscape of pure anxiety. SUBHEAD: The New Wave of Minimal Survival Horror

sections.content: Frozen helped pave the way for other stripped-down survival films like Fall (2022) and Beast (2022). These films share a commitment to psychological realism and practical effects over CGI spectacle. The success of these smaller-scale horror thrillers proves audiences connect deeply with relatable characters facing seemingly impossible odds.
